entries.sentence: A common condition in which fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.
entries.note: NHS: common condition where fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.

entries.sentence: Fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems is now called MASLD and was formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).
entries.note: Both pages say NAFLD is the older name and MASLD the new one.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes.
entries.note: NHS: can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes.

entries.sentence: It does not usually cause symptoms and is often found through tests done for another reason.
entries.note: NHS: usually no symptoms, found by tests for something else; BLT: often found during tests for something else.

entries.sentence: The British Liver Trust says most cases stay mild, but in a small number of people the condition can progress to scarring, cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.
entries.note: BLT summary: most cases stay mild; small number progress to scarring, cirrhosis, liver failure, liver cancer.

entries.sentence: Fat builds up in the liver, often in people who are overweight.
entries.note: NHS: fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.

entries.sentence: Obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes raise the risk.
entries.note: NIDDK summary: obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes raise risk.

entries.sentence: Gene variants that increase the risk have been found in research funded by NIDDK.
entries.note: NIDDK blog summary: NIDDK-funded research found gene variants that increase risk.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and alcohol intake and measures height, weight and waist.
Further blood tests or an ultrasound scan may follow, to confirm fat in the liver, rule out other causes and check for liver damage.

entries.note: NHS: lifestyle change is the core treatment.

entries.sentence: People without liver damage do not usually need specialist care, whereas those with fibrosis or cirrhosis are seen by a liver specialist.
The NHS mentions pioglitazone or vitamin E as options in that setting.
The British Liver Trust adds that medicines may be used for linked conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
The British Liver Trust gives a healthy diet, regular physical activity and a healthy weight as the first approach.
The NHS also advises not smoking.
entries.note: NHS lifestyle advice, per search summary.

entries.sentence: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP urgently, or calling NHS 111, for jaundice, itchy skin or swelling of the legs or abdomen in someone with a known liver condition.
MedlinePlus lists persistent tiredness or pain in the upper right abdomen as reasons for assessment, and a routine GP appointment is the usual first step in the UK.
entries.note: MedlinePlus: persistent fatigue or upper-right abdominal pain warrant assessment. Second clause is general UK routing.

entries.sentence: Vomiting blood or collapse is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.
entries.note: General emergency routing, not from retrieved text.

entries.sentence: Fatty liver disease means fat has built up in the liver, and the NHS says it is a common condition.
The name has changed over time: it was long called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and the British Liver Trust now uses metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD.
entries.note: BLT: NAFLD is the older name.

entries.sentence: Its more serious form, in which the liver is also inflamed, is now called MASH and was previously called NASH.
NIDDK describes simple fatty liver and the inflamed form as two types of the same disease.
entries.note: NIDDK: NAFL and NASH are types of NAFLD.

entries.sentence: NHS hospital leaflets describe four stages: simple fatty liver, inflammation, scarring and cirrhosis.
entries.note: Search summary: most sources describe four stages (steatosis, MASH, fibrosis, cirrhosis).

entries.sentence: In cirrhosis the liver shrinks and becomes scarred and lumpy, and the damage is permanent.
The British Liver Trust estimates that about 1 in 4 adults in the UK have MASLD.
A 2023 consensus statement it cites puts the figure at up to 1 in 3.
The NHS says fatty liver disease does not usually cause symptoms.
NIDDK calls it a silent disease with few or no symptoms.
It is therefore often found through blood tests or scans done for another reason.
Some people feel very tired or generally unwell, according to the NHS.
Others notice discomfort in the upper right side of the abdomen, under the ribs.
entries.note: NHS: discomfort under right side of ribs.

entries.sentence: MedlinePlus lists persistent tiredness or upper right abdominal pain among reasons for assessment.
NHS hospital leaflets note that some symptoms may come from linked conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea or heart disease.
In advanced disease, yellow skin and eyes (jaundice) or swelling of the ankles and abdomen can appear.
NIDDK warns, on its page for children, that by the time symptoms arise there may already be permanent liver damage.
The NHS says a GP will ask about symptoms and about how much alcohol a person drinks.
The GP also measures height, weight and waist size.
Further blood tests or an ultrasound scan may follow, to confirm fat in the liver, to rule out other causes and to look for liver damage.
NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form.
A patient information sheet used in the NHS says a biopsy is sometimes needed, mainly when the diagnosis is in doubt or cirrhosis is a concern.
Fibrosis means scarring of the liver.
NICE recommends that people with NAFLD are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis.
It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered.
NICE material advises that adults and young people found to have advanced fibrosis are referred to a liver specialist.
entries.note: Evidence document: refer to a relevant hepatology specialist.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes lifestyle change as the main treatment.
That means a balanced diet, regular exercise and weight loss for people who are overweight.
NIDDK also names weight loss as the main recommendation, because it can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring.
The British Liver Trust cites evidence that losing 5 to 10 per cent of body weight can control the condition and in some cases reverse it.
The NHS advises regular check-ups for people without liver damage, at least once a year.
People without liver damage do not usually need specialist care.
When fibrosis or cirrhosis is present, a liver specialist becomes involved, and the NHS mentions pioglitazone or vitamin E as options.
MedlinePlus describes resmetirom, used with diet and exercise, for adults with NASH without cirrhosis who have moderate to advanced scarring.
NIDDK says certain diabetes medicines can effectively improve NASH.
The British Liver Trust adds that medicines may treat linked conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
The NHS lists type 2 diabetes among the risk factors for fatty liver disease.
NIDDK says obesity and type 2 diabetes both raise the chance that simple fatty liver progresses to inflammation and scarring.
The link runs both ways: one review reports that people with MASLD have a two to five times higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes than the general population.
The same review reports that diabetes in people with MASLD is linked to a higher risk of serious liver complications and of liver cancer.
entries.note: Review: >2-fold risk of hepatic decompensation, >5-fold HCC.

entries.sentence: In a study of repeated liver biopsies, type 2 diabetes was linked to a higher risk of scarring getting worse.
entries.note: Search summary: paired biopsies, 70 percent higher relative risk.

entries.sentence: One review describes the disease as a spectrum running from simple fatty liver through inflammation to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
Authors of reviews recommend finding MASLD early in people with diabetes.
The British Liver Trust says most cases stay mild.
It also says a small number of people progress to serious liver disease.
The trust points to weight loss as something that can, in some cases, reverse the condition.
The NHS adds that, without liver damage, specialist care is not usually needed.
The trust also runs a free, nurse-led helpline for people with liver conditions.
NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP urgently, or calling NHS 111, for jaundice, itchy skin or swelling of the legs or abdomen in someone with a known liver condition.
Persistent tiredness or pain under the right ribs would normally be raised at a routine GP appointment.
entries.note: MedlinePlus says assessment is warranted; routine routing is general UK practice.

entries.sentence: Vomiting blood or collapse is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.
The NHS says it can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes.
The British Liver Trust cites evidence that losing 5 to 10 per cent of body weight can control the condition and sometimes reverse it.
NIDDK says weight loss can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring.
Established cirrhosis damage is described in NHS leaflets as permanent.
MASLD is the newer name for what was called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD.
The inflamed form, MASH, was previously called NASH.
The British Liver Trust says steatotic liver disease is now used as an umbrella term for the various causes of fat in the liver.
Some older pages and leaflets still use the earlier names.
entries.note: BLT: older pages still use NAFLD.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a GP asks about alcohol intake when assessing the liver.
One NHS hospital leaflet advises avoiding alcohol and describes MASLD as associated with being overweight or obese, or having diabetes.
entries.note: Search summary of leaflet; page identity of leaflet not certain.

entries.sentence: Blood tests or an ultrasound scan may also be used to rule out other causes of fat build-up.
entries.note: NHS: further tests rule out other causes.
